title: Why Use Lindel?
description: Lindel — *linearization with delight* — maps multi-dimensional points onto a single integer that follows a [Hilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_curve) or [Morton (Z-order)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z-order_curve) space-filling curve. Used as the `ORDER BY` key when writing Parquet, it's the same [Z-Order / liquid-clustering](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/delta/clustering) optimization Databricks pioneered for Delta Lake.

sections.title: One sort key for every dimension at once
sections.description: Parquet readers prune work using per-row-group min/max statistics — but sorting a file by a single column gives you tight bounds on *that* column only; every other column ends up scattered across row groups, so a predicate on it can't skip anything. A space-filling curve sidesteps this: it collapses N dimensions into one ordering where points that were close in the original space stay close in the file. Sort by that one key and a multi-column predicate gets meaningful per-row-group bounds on *all* of its columns simultaneously, not just the first sort column. The same coordinate-locality also helps the encoders — adjacent rows have adjacent values, so RLE, dictionary, and delta encodings inside each row group find more runs and shorter deltas, and files shrink.

sections.title: Hilbert vs Morton
sections.description: Both curves are *locality-preserving* and both reduce to bit manipulation over the input dimensions, but they trade locality against throughput. Pick Hilbert by default; pick Morton when encoding speed is the bottleneck.

bulletPoints.label: Hilbert — better locality
bulletPoints.description: The [Hilbert curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_curve) never makes long jumps in input space: consecutive positions along the curve are always neighbours in N-D. That yields tighter row-group bounding boxes at the cost of slightly more CPU per encode. The geometry indexing systems [S2](https://s2geometry.io/) (Google) and [H3](https://h3geo.org/) (Uber) use Hilbert-style ordering for the same reason, and Delta Lake's [liquid clustering](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/delta/clustering) moved to it.

bulletPoints.label: Morton — faster, simpler
bulletPoints.description: The [Morton / Z-order curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z-order_curve) is plain bit-interleaving of the input dimensions — trivially cheap to compute, but with occasional long jumps at quadrant boundaries that loosen the bounding boxes. The [Bing Maps Tile System](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/bingmaps/articles/bing-maps-tile-system) uses Morton-style quadkeys, and Delta Lake's original `ZORDER BY` was Morton.

bulletPoints.label: Output width follows the inputs
bulletPoints.description: Both encoders are polymorphic over `UTINYINT` through `UHUGEINT`. The result is the smallest unsigned integer that fits *bit-width × dimensions* — e.g. two 32-bit dimensions (64 bits total) return a `UBIGINT`, three return a `UHUGEINT`.

sections.title: What to know before you sort by it
sections.description: A few honest caveats so you give the curve the right inputs and reach for it in the right situation.

bulletPoints.label: Inputs are unsigned integers
bulletPoints.description: The curves only carry the bits they're handed, and locality is driven by the high bits of each dimension. Quantize floats first (`(lat * 1e6)::UINTEGER` gives ~10 cm resolution worldwide) and map signed ranges to unsigned, pre-scaling so the precision you care about lands in those high bits.

bulletPoints.label: Skew can dominate the ordering
bulletPoints.description: If one input column has far higher cardinality or a far wider range than the others, it dominates the encoded key and the locality benefit on the other columns collapses. Rescale the dimensions to comparable ranges before encoding, or drop the dominant column from the curve and add it as a secondary `ORDER BY` term.

bulletPoints.label: Decoding doesn't carry types
bulletPoints.description: Reconstructing the original array needs the dimension count, float-ness, and signed-ness passed explicitly — none of that is stored in the encoded integer, so the decode call has to be told the shape the value originally had.

bulletPoints.label: It's a write-time ordering, not an index
bulletPoints.description: The gain comes entirely from how rows are laid out in the Parquet file, so it only helps data written in encoded order. There is no live index to maintain: updating means rewriting the affected files, and for streaming inserts you batch and re-sort on a cadence rather than expecting one row at a time to improve skipping. Real-world speedups depend on data shape and filter selectivity — the regime [Delta Lake liquid clustering](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/delta/clustering) targets.
